research_concepts: role stability / transferability (consistency of individual player performance profile across different team contexts)
structural role (the functional niche a player occupies in an offense)
methodological_questions: How to operationally define 'cut-heavy' vs 'drive-heavy' from play-type possession records?
How to quantify 'role' in a way that captures the structural influence of a shaper?
What constitutes a 'travel' event: change of team, coach, system, season?
How to measure 'travels better': smaller within-player role distance after a context change?
What confounders (age, contract year, injury, team talent) could produce spurious differences in role stability?
What sample size is required to detect a practically meaningful difference in role stability between groups?
evidence_establishes: No prior evidence from this project was retrieved; the question has not been studied internally before.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether cut-heavy shapers' roles are more stable than drive-heavy ones.
What the typical effect size of play-style on role portability is.
How to reliably classify shapers into cut-heavy vs drive-heavy from available data.
own_inferences: The question implies a causal-comparative design: differing play-style (cut vs drive) is the independent variable, and role stability across contexts is the dependent variable.

Operationalizing 'shaper' likely requires filtering for high-usage or high-possession-initiation players; 'cut-heavy' vs 'drive-heavy' can be defined by the proportion of initiated possessions that are cuts vs drives, using the graph database of play-type records.

'Travels better' can be measured as the within-player similarity (e.g., 1 - Euclidean distance) of z-scored offensive role metrics (usage, assist rate, shot frequency by zone, turnover rate, points per possession) between consecutive seasons or pre/post trade, comparing the average similarity between groups.

A major threat is regression to the mean: if a shaper is classified as extreme on a dichotomized continuous measure (cut frequency), their subsequent role stability may be inflated by measurement error, not true portability.
Confounding by player quality, age, contract status, and team offensive style could easily dominate; with only ~24 units, adequate control is unlikely.

The stated n=24 likely refers to the number of shapers who both changed teams during the observation window and meet inclusion criteria; this is very small for detecting a between-group difference in stability.
uncertainties: The exact operational definitions of 'shaper', 'cut-heavy', 'drive-heavy', and 'role' are not yet specified and will influence testability.
The number of 'travel' events (team changes) available in the data may be larger than 24 if mid-season trades are fully exploited, but the stated n=24 suggests a preliminary count.
The reliability and completeness of the derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type) are unknown.
Whether there is a large enough pool of cut-heavy shapers (who also change teams) for a meaningful comparison.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical evidence was retrieved, so the decision is based entirely on the current feasibility assessment.

blocking_constraints.text: n=24 is insufficient to detect a plausible between-group difference in role stability with adequate power, even for a large effect.
The exposure of interest (shaper changing teams) is rare; combined with the need to split into cut-heavy and drive-heavy, cell sizes may drop below 10.
Cut/drive classification from derived play-type records may be noisy, and role distance metrics have unknown reliability across team contexts.
Dichotomizing a continuous play-style variable (e.g., cut%) risks selecting extreme groups that regress toward the mean in subsequent role measures, biasing the comparison.
Reasons for team change (trade vs free agency, injury, decline) differ systematically by play style and age, confounding the relationship with subsequent role stability.

prior_work.summary: No earlier project studies were retrieved, so it is unknown whether the question has been substantially answered previously.

risks.text: The projected n=24 likely yields low statistical power for a between-group comparison of continuous stability scores, especially after controlling for confounders.
The intersection of 'shapers who changed teams' and the cut/drive dichotomy may yield very small groups, increasing vulnerability to outliers.
Reliability of the play-type classification and the derived role distance measure could be low, especially if some play types (e.g., cuts) are less frequent and more prone to misclassification.
Classifying players as cut-heavy based on a single season's data exaggerates the extremity of the group, causing role stability to appear higher or lower spuriously.
Age, contract status, injury, and team offensive system all influence both play-style classification and role stability; with small n adjustment is difficult.
If role stability is measured on many dimensions (scoring efficiency, playmaking, rebounding, usage), multiple comparisons will inflate false positive risk.
If play-style classification and role stability use data from the same season, independence is violated; a temporal split is necessary.

design.estimand: ATE of being a cut-heavy (vs drive-heavy) shaper on within-player role stability (Euclidean distance between standardized offensive performance vectors) across different team contexts.
design.unit: player-season-to-season transition where the player changed teams, for players classified as shapers.
design.sample: All players with usage rate > 20% and >500 total possessions initiated in the season prior to a team change, spanning 2022-23 through 2025-26 regular seasons and playoffs. Play-style classification: cut-heavy if >40% of initiated possessions are 'cut' play types; drive-heavy if >30% are 'drive' play types and <20% are 'cut' (mutually exclusive groups, with an excluded mixed group). Minimum 20 games played in both pre- and post-change seasons.
design.power: With an estimated n=24 (12 per group) and a plausible standardized effect size d=0.4, power for a two-sample t-test at alpha=0.05 is approximately 0.15-0.25. To achieve 0.80 power would require n≈100 per group.
design.controls: Age (at time of change), minutes per game in pre-change season, team offensive rating in pre-change season, injury-related games missed, whether the change was in-season (trade) or off-season, and whether the player changed conferences.
design.falsification: Test whether role stability in a control set of shapers who stayed with the same team shows the same cut-vs-drive difference; if the effect is identical, the travel claim is falsified. Also, check if the result holds when classification is based on career-long play-type frequencies rather than the single pre-change season.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register a single composite measure of role distance (e.g., Mahalanobis distance on a fixed set of core offensive metrics) and a single primary test. Any exploratory breakdowns by individual metrics will be reported with unadjusted p-values and flagged as secondary.
design.decision_rule: Not applicable (do_not_proceed). A minimum viable test would require a sample size of at least 60 per group and a validated, dimension-reduced measure of offensive role.
design.data_version: Per-game NBA stats API files and derived play-type possession graph database as of 2026-08-08.

methodological_questions: How to define cut-heavy vs drive-heavy shapers?
How to measure that a role 'travels' better (transferability, stability across contexts)?
What are the confounders in comparing transferability across different play styles?
What sample size is needed to detect differences in role stability?

Research question (as posed on 2026-08-08, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=24

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

"Roles travel better" might refer to how well a player's role or style transfers across different contexts (e.g., different teams, different lineups, different seasons? Possibly "travel" meaning how well a player's impact or role stability persists across different settings? The research question is in the area of "structural roles and influence". Might be about how players' offensive roles (defined by cut frequency vs drive frequency) translate across different team contexts or across seasons? The data available spans multiple seasons (2022-23 through 2025-26) so it could involve season-to-season stability or cross-context transfer. The term "shapers" likely refers to players who shape the offense. We should identify relevant research concepts: maybe "role stability", "play style transferability", "off-ball movement" (cutting), "on-ball driving", "structural role", "role portability". Methodological questions: How to define cut-heavy vs drive-heavy? How to measure "travel" (stability, transfer across teams/lineups, predictive accuracy)? Sample size: n=24 units available. That's small; might refer to something like 24 players? Or 24 team-seasons? We need to retrieve history with these concepts.

We'll craft research_concepts as a list of strings: e.g., ["cutting", "driving", "role stability", "role transferability", "structural role", "off-ball movement", "on-ball creation"]. Methodological questions: ["how to measure role portability?", "definitions of cut-heavy vs drive-heavy", "sample size requirements for role stability analyses", "confounders in comparing role transfer across playing styles"]. Query: a concise summary: "Do cut-heavy shapers' roles transfer better than drive-heavy shapers?".

Let's construct the args.

We are now in Stage 2. The retrieval returned no results. So we have no historical evidence from this project. We need to proceed with steps 4-9 using only the task statement, data catalog, glossary, and our own reasoning. We must output the required JSON.

We need to assess the research question: "Cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones." The area is structural roles and influence. The data available includes per-game files from NBA stats API, play-by-play, substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary, and derived play-type possession records in a graph database. Units available: n=24. Not sure what "n=24" refers to—likely the number of players that fit the "shapers" definition? Or teams? We need to clarify: 24 units could be players, teams, or roles. The question compares "cut-heavy shapers" vs "drive-heavy shapers". "Shapers" might be players who shape the offense, e.g., primary initiators or high-usage players. The claim: roles travel better for cut-heavy than drive-heavy players. "Travel better" likely means that the player's role (e.g., offensive impact, play style) is more stable or transfers better when the player changes team, coach, season, or context. But the data spans multiple seasons, so we could measure within-player role stability across seasons or compare across contexts (e.g., different team). But the question is causal/comparative: cut-heavy players' roles are more portable than drive-heavy players'.

We need to define concepts: "cut-heavy shaper", "drive-heavy shaper", "role", "travel better". This is a structural roles question about influence. Shapers presumably influence the game, maybe high-usage players who create shots for themselves and others. "Cut-heavy" means they primarily move without the ball, cutting to the basket; "drive-heavy" means they primarily create off the dribble, driving to the basket. Both are shapers, but with different play styles. The hypothesis is that roles (perhaps offensive role, like usage, playmaking, scoring efficiency, etc.) are more consistent across different environments for cut-heavy shapers than for drive-heavy shapers. So we need to define a measure of role, and then measure stability/transferability. Potential confounders: age, team system, coach, teammates, injury. Need to define a "travel" event: a player changing teams or a coach changing, etc. With multiple seasons, we could look at players who changed teams between seasons. But sample size (n=24) might limit power. Also, defining cut-heavy vs drive-heavy requires a threshold on a continuous metric, leading to risk of regression to the mean (RTM) and selection issues.

We should identify methodological questions: how to measure role, how to measure travel/transferability, how to control for confounding, sample size concerns.

Now we need to produce output. Since no historical evidence, historical_evidence and failed_approaches are empty. evidence_establishes and evidence_does_not_establish reflect that no prior work was retrieved.

We need to make a decision: proceed, proceed_with_changes, or do_not_proceed. We need to weigh testability, risks, predicted outcome. Let's think about the feasibility.

First, define "shapers": likely players with high usage rate (USG%) or high assists. The NBA stats API provides box-score summary, which includes usage, assists, etc. But "shapers" might be defined via the graph database of play-type possession records: initiator, play type. So we can identify players who initiate many possessions (isolation, pick-and-roll ball handler, etc.) and distinguish between cutting (off-ball cuts) and driving (drives). The play-by-play data includes action type, sub-type. Cuts and drives can be identified from play-by-play or derived possession data. The graph database includes "initiator, play type, points". So we can classify players as cut-heavy or drive-heavy based on their play-type distribution.

Next, "role": could be defined as the player's statistical profile: e.g., points per possession, assist rate, turnover rate, usage, shot distribution, etc. "Travel better" means the role remains stable when context changes (e.g., changing teams). We need a "travel" event: player changing teams between seasons. The data covers multiple seasons: 2022-23 to 2025-26. So we can identify players who played for different teams in consecutive seasons. Unit: player. n=24 likely refers to the number of shapers who have changed teams and fit the classification? With 5 seasons, we might have many players, but limiting to "shapers" who changed teams and have enough minutes could yield maybe 20-30, so n=24 plausible.

But comparing stability: we need a measure of role distance between seasons for the same player in different environments. Then test whether the average distance is smaller for cut-heavy than drive-heavy. However, many confounds: players who change teams might be older, different talent levels, injuries, role changes due to team fit. Also, cut-heavy players might be less ball-dominant and thus have more stable roles because they rely less on having the ball, while drive-heavy players need the ball more, so their role might depend more on teammates and system. But that's the hypothesis. To test, we need to control for things like minutes, team offensive rating, etc. But with small n, controlling many covariates is difficult.

Risks: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (n=24 likely low power), EXPOSURE_SPARSITY (few shapers with clearly defined cut-heavy vs drive-heavy and multiple team changes), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (defining cut/drive from play-by-play; reliability?), RTM_SELECTION (classifying based on a single season's cut/drive frequency could lead to regression to the mean when looking at role stability in next season), CONFOUNDING (age, contract status, injury, team system), BASE_RATE (how many shapers change teams? maybe few), MULTIPLE_TESTING (if we test many role dimensions). Also, the outcome "role stability" might be derived from the same data used to classify, leading to leakage or mechanical correlations. But we could use one season to classify and a different season to measure stability, but still RTM issues.

LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD: if we define cut-heavy based on the entire sample period, we might inadvertently use future info, but we can avoid that.

OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL: not exactly a label, but the role distance could be noisy.

The question is testable in principle, but with low power due to small n. The n=24 given might be the maximum number of eligible shapers. If we can increase n by including other seasons or using within-season changes (e.g., trades mid-season) then n could be larger. But the data includes in-season trades? Play-by-play data per game allows tracking players across teams within a season. So we could look at players who were traded mid-season. That could increase sample.

But still, testability might be low. I'd estimate p_testable around 0.3. Decision: do_not_proceed due to insufficient sample and high risk of confounds, or proceed_with_changes to a descriptive pilot study. The instructions say to make a decision and provide design even if do_not_proceed. We'll output a reasoned recommendation.

testability: p_testable: 0.25 (low power, many risks). blocking_constraints: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, CONFOUNDING, RTM_SELECTION.

risks: list relevant risk codes.

predicted_outcome: based on reasoning, I think it's likely an adequately powered test would be untestable due to insufficient data, and even if tested, could be uncertain or artifact. So probabilities: supported: 0.1, rejected: 0.1, untestable: 0.5, artifact: 0.2, uncertain: 0.1. Sum to 1.

decision: do_not_proceed. But we still provide a design.

Design: estimand: "Difference in role stability (e.g., Euclidean distance between standardized performance metrics in consecutive seasons) between cut-heavy and drive-heavy shapers, conditional on a change of team context." unit: "player (shaper)". sample: "NBA shapers (e.g., players with usage > 20% and total possessions initiated > 500) who changed teams between 2022-23 and 2025-26 seasons (including mid-season trades), classified as cut-heavy or drive-heavy based on prior-season play-type frequencies." power: "With n~24, power to detect a medium standardized effect size (d=0.5) is approximately 30-40%, insufficient." controls: "age, minutes, team offensive rating, injury status." falsification: "Check that role stability in seasons without team change is similar for both groups (if enough data)." multiplicity: "If testing multiple role dimensions, apply Bonferroni correction."
